purpose: Compare public TLS echo workloads with a colocated router and relay, then control VM placement by sending the backend through a self-targeted HTTPS peer integration.

benchmarkBuild.method: go build overlay replacing e2e/pathbench/main.go with the pinned source

environment.directory: Private loopback with a fresh test token; independent of the live directory

workload.order: integration or separate first on repetitions 1 and 3; colocated first on repetition 2
workload.driverLocation: A separate Mac; both client and echo host are outside the tested VMs
workload.registration: SSH forwards to node listeners pin the serving node; all measured connect and accept traffic uses the public WSS endpoint
workload.payloadIntegrity: Every echo validates its length, sequence and payload bytes
workload.resources: 0.5-second samples within the driver measurement timestamps; CPU is percent of one core; network counters are VM-wide eth0 only
workload.summary: Each displayed quantity is the median of three run-level quantities, including p99

limitations: This is a bounded workload comparison, not a maximum capacity, long-duration or failover test.
Live VMs and the fresh VM have different scheduling conditions; the same-VM control fixes placement but reported CPU steal still varies by path.
The self-targeted peer integration exercises the HTTPS integration transport without a second relay VM. It does not reproduce every cross-VM latency component.
eth0 excludes the loopback connection between the public proxy and the application. Near-zero eth0 traffic does not mean near-zero public traffic.
The source driver sends both halves of each echo over its external connection, and may cap higher-load throughput.
